claims.text: Toughness retention in HEAs is governed by the stability of coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates at or near grain boundaries promote crack deflection and crack blunting.
Thermal treatments that dissolve coherent nanoscale precipitates cause a loss of toughness relative to the baseline state.
Standard processing produces an HEA microstructure containing a stable distribution of coherent nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries.
Annealing above the critical temperature for precipitate stability will dissolve or coarsen the nanoscale precipitates.
The relevant structural mediator is the volume fraction and morphology of coherent nanoscale precipitates, particularly those at or near grain boundaries.
Coherent precipitates promote local plastic deformation.
Dissolution or coarsening of the precipitates removes the effective crack-blunting mechanism.
Loss of the precipitate-mediated crack-blunting mechanism diminishes toughness.
High-temperature-annealed samples will exhibit lower impact energy or fracture toughness than the baseline samples.

The hypothesis is limited to similar alloy systems and processing windows in which precipitate dissolution or coarsening is the primary microstructural change and no other significant phase transformation occurs.
The critical temperature for precipitate instability and the magnitude of toughness loss depend on alloy composition and annealing schedule.
Failure to observe a significant toughness reduction after confirmed precipitate dissolution or coarsening would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
